text: Rarely is a maritime casualty caused by a single failure.

Candidates lose marks in three places, and only one of them is vocabulary. The first is degree. The text says rarely and the option says never, and because the topic is identical the eye accepts it. The second is agency. The text says the figures must have been produced from another plan, and the option says the operator produced them from another plan, and the difference is the whole sentence. The third is register. The text says the vessel ran aground and the option says the vessel became hard-fast, and the candidate rejects the right answer precisely because it does not look like the text. If you fix those three, you do not need to read faster. You already read well enough.

I have signed hundreds of drill records and I have watched perhaps a third of the drills they describe. That is the whole problem in one sentence. On paper we hold a lifeboat drill every month and every person on board has a muster station. In practice, a drill that takes eleven minutes and ends with everyone back at work has taught nobody anything. What I look for now is different. I want to see somebody sent to the wrong station on purpose. I want the list to be wrong and somebody to notice. And I want the near miss written down even when nothing happened, because the near miss is the only honest record we keep. Nobody is ever punished for an accident that did not occur, which is exactly why people will tell you about it.
